hints: Start by sorting the five descriptions into two groups - those about the whole system type and vessel types, and those about named heart structures.
For the first row, think what it means if blood stays inside vessels all the time and visits the heart twice per circuit - what two words describe closedness and doubleness.
For the tiny $7 \mu m$ vessel, recall which vessel is just wide enough for one red blood cell to squeeze through and is the site of exchange with cells.
For the vessel from lungs to heart, remember the rule that veins carry blood toward the heart - which vein is the exception that carries oxygenated blood.
For the last two rows, picture the heart in section - which upper chamber receives vena cava blood, and what wall prevents mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood.
walkthrough:
Name the whole system type**
Mammals keep blood always inside vessels, so it is a closed system. Because blood passes through the heart twice - once on the pulmonary circuit to the lungs and once on the systemic circuit to the body - in one complete circuit, it is a closed double circulation.

Spot the exchange vessel**
A lumen of about $7 \mu m$ is capillary size. Capillaries have very thin walls, one cell thick, and form networks close to cells, so they are the vessels that supply substances to cells and remove waste.

Trace oxygenated blood back to the heart**
Blood picks up oxygen in the lungs and must return to the left atrium. Any vessel carrying blood toward the heart is a vein, so this is the pulmonary vein. It is unusual because most veins carry deoxygenated blood.

Locate where body blood enters**
Deoxygenated blood from the body arrives via the vena cava into the upper right chamber. That receiving chamber is the right atrium, which then passes blood to the right ventricle for pumping to the lungs.

Identify the divider**
The muscular wall that divides the heart into left and right sides and prevents mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood is the septum.
Final answer: closed double circulation; capillary; pulmonary vein; right atrium; septum.

hints: Think about what blood plasma mostly is, and what must happen to a substance like a salt, sugar or amino acid before blood can carry it from one place to another.
Recall why water is good at this - its polarity lets it surround ions and polar molecules - and link this to named examples carried in mammalian blood.
walkthrough:
Link solvent to transport**
Blood is mostly water in the plasma. For the circulatory system to move nutrients, salts, waste and proteins, those substances need to be carried in solution, dissolved in that water.

Show what dissolves and why it matters**
Because water is polar, it can surround and separate charged particles. So ionic compounds dissociate, polar compounds like glucose and amino acids dissolve, and hydrophilic globular proteins stay in solution. That is how the mammalian transport system moves them to and from cells.

Final answer: Many transported substances must be dissolved in solution to be carried in blood plasma; water dissolves ions, polar molecules such as glucose and amino acids, and globular proteins such as antibodies/hormones.

hints: Start from the bond itself - water molecules attract each other by a specific weak bond - and give the special names for water sticking to water versus water sticking to walls.
Think what happens at the leaf when water evaporates from mesophyll and leaves the top of the xylem - how would pulling on the top molecule affect the ones below if they are all linked.
Now think about gravity pulling down on a tall column of water - what interaction with the hydrophilic cellulose wall of the xylem helps hold the column up.
walkthrough:
Cohesion from hydrogen bonds**
Water molecules are attracted to each other by hydrogen bonds. This attraction between like water molecules is called cohesion, so water in the xylem behaves as a linked chain rather than separate molecules.

Cohesion creates the pull**
When water evaporates from leaves and leaves the xylem at the top, it tugs on the molecule below. Because of cohesion, that pull is transmitted down the chain, drawing a continuous stream of water up the xylem. This is the transpiration pull.

Adhesion holds the column up**
Water also forms hydrogen bonds with the walls of the xylem, which is adhesion to the hydrophilic cellulose lining. Adhesion plus cohesion maintains an unbroken column of water and stops it falling back down under gravity, allowing movement to the top of the plant.

Final answer: Hydrogen bonding gives cohesion between water molecules so evaporation/transpiration pull at the top pulls water molecules below upward; adhesion to hydrophilic cellulose/lignin lining of xylem maintains an unbroken column of water.
